Strongest to weakest: (1) the 300-case evaluation set built from your own invoices, because it measures the configuration you will ship on the distribution you serve; (2) the replicated academic result on a public extraction benchmark, because it is independent and reproducible, though the benchmark may differ from your documents; (3) the vendor blog post, which is a claim under conditions that favor the vendor and may hide prompt format, sampling, or tool use; (4) the colleague's impression, which shows a capability may exist and nothing about frequency. The ranking is by independence and reproducibility, with the special status of your own set coming from its match to your workload rather than from its methodology.

K6. The registry version records what you intended to send; the content hash records what was actually sent after rendering. They diverge whenever the rendered prompt depends on request data: an interpolated date, a tenant name, a retrieved snippet, a feature flag. For debugging you need the hash (two requests with the same hash and different answers isolate model nondeterminism); for change management you need the version (pass rate before and after prompt version 7). Storing only one loses the other question.

docs.title: Engineering questions
docs.text:
E1. Twelve categories, routing to a queue: the information needed is in the ticket text itself, so stop at rung one, a prompt with an output schema that constrains the category to the twelve allowed values, plus deterministic routing code keyed on the category. Build a labeled evaluation set (a few hundred historical tickets with human labels) and measure accuracy per category. Evidence to climb: if per-category accuracy is poor on categories whose definitions depend on internal knowledge (for example, "billing" versus "contracts" depends on product names only Northwind uses), retrieval of category definitions or examples (rung two) is justified. If accuracy remains systematically wrong on the same confusable pairs after prompt and few-shot work, and volume is high enough that a small tuned classifier would cut cost, fine-tuning (the side branch off the ladder) is justified. Tools and agents are not: nothing needs to be read from a live system and the path is fixed.

E2. Required justification: a named decision the agent would make that cannot be enumerated as a workflow branch; an evaluation set where the current workflow measurably fails because of that decision; a projection of added latency, cost, and attack surface; and a budget and termination design. The baseline to beat: identity, permission-aware hybrid retrieval over all sources at once (so "which source to search" disappears as a decision), rerank, generation with citations, evidence gate, and a deterministic clarifying-question branch triggered when the gate finds evidence from conflicting documents or the query is below a length or specificity threshold. If that baseline passes the evaluation set, the agent is not justified; if it fails only on cases that require sequential dependent lookups, the agent's scope is exactly those cases.

E3. Dropped: evidence and index_version (no retrieval), tools (none offered), and the evidence-related gate. Retained: request_id, tenant, principal and groups (an invoice belongs to a tenant), model, prompt, usage, latency_ms, output_hash, output_kind (an extraction that failed validation and went to the review queue is a fallback, not an answer), gates (schema validation and any PII scan are gates), eval_outcome. New essential field: an input identity, such as a hash or document id of the invoice that was extracted from, together with the schema version of the output. Without the input identity you cannot replay or compare; without the schema version you cannot tell a model regression from a schema change. A repair-attempt count is also useful for cost analysis.

E4. Filtering before ranking means the candidate set never contains a document the caller may not see, so no downstream component can be influenced by it. A post-ranking filter admits restricted documents into the candidate set, where they can leak in several ways even if removed before generation: a reranker trained to use cross-document context can shift scores; a query-expansion or multi-query step may generate follow-up queries from restricted content; a "related documents" or "did you mean" feature may surface titles; result counts and latency can differ in ways that reveal the document's existence; and a bug in the filter stage turns into a leak rather than a search miss. One concrete leak: the pipeline returns "I found 3 documents but you may not see 2 of them" or logs their titles into a trace the user can later request.

docs.title: Practical exercises
docs.text:
P1. Expected implementation: add a StageLatency dataclass (name: str, ms: float) and a stages: list[StageLatency] field on RequestLineage; add dominant_stage() -> str | None returning the stage with the largest ms, or None if no stages were recorded; optionally extend unanswered_questions to report "per-stage latency" when stages is empty. Acceptance: a test where retrieval is 1,400 ms, rerank 300 ms, model 500 ms, gates 40 ms asserts dominant_stage() == "retrieval"; a test asserts the sum of stages does not exceed latency_ms (or flags it as a violation); the round-trip test still passes with the new field serialized.

P2. Expected implementation: completeness_report(records: list[RequestLineage]) -> dict[str, float] that calls unanswered_questions() on each record, counts occurrences per question string, and divides by len(records); questions never missing appear with 0.0; an empty input returns an empty dict or raises, documented either way. Acceptance: with four records of which one lacks gates and two lack usage, the report shows 0.25 for "which policy gates ran" and 0.5 for "how many tokens it consumed" and 0.0 for the others.

P3. Expected implementation: in consistency_violations, for each ToolEvent with outcome == "pending_approval", look for a PolicyGate whose name identifies the approval gate for that tool (for example f"approval:{tool.name}" or a gate carrying the tool name in its reason) and report a violation if its decision is allow. Also report a violation if a pending_approval tool has no approval gate recorded at all. Acceptance: the failing test is written first with ToolEvent("send_reply", offered=True, called=True, outcome="pending_approval") and PolicyGate("approval:send_reply", "allow"), asserts a violation naming send_reply, fails on the current code, then passes after the change; existing tests remain green.

P4. Expected diagram: a flowchart TD with the ticket text entering a context layer that holds only "render classification prompt vN", a model layer with the gateway and model, an action layer marked as absent or degenerate (no tools offered), a control layer marked single pass, and an operations layer with schema validation gate, trace, and eval. The trust boundary sits around the model: ticket text is untrusted input (it may contain injected instructions), and the only thing crossing back is a category constrained to twelve values by schema validation before deterministic routing code uses it. A good answer marks the ticket text as subgraph Untrusted.

docs.title: Debugging exercises
docs.text:
D1. Root cause: the evidence gate's condition is wrong or vacuous. With evidence = [] it should have decided deny or escalate; it decided allow, most likely because the check is "all cited chunks are in the context" and a model output with zero citations passes vacuously, or because the relevance threshold is compared against a default score when no chunks exist. The layer is operations (gate logic), not model or context; the model did what an ungated model does. The revealing trace fields are the pair evidence = [] with evidence_gate: allow; a consistency check "evidence gate may not allow when evidence is empty" would have flagged it at request time. Fix the gate to require at least one chunk above threshold and at least one citation, and add that check to consistency_violations.

D2. Most likely cause: a silent provider-side model change behind an unchanged model name (or a change in a provider default such as sampling or a safety filter). Everything you version is constant, and the one thing you do not control is the only remaining variable. The lineage design allowed it to go undetected because model.version is null: the record names the model but not the snapshot, so the change is invisible in traces. Two changes: (1) record the provider's returned model identifier or snapshot tag per response where the API exposes one, and where it does not, pin to a dated model alias and record it; (2) run the offline evaluation set on a schedule independent of deploys (daily against production configuration), with an alert on pass-rate drops, so a drift with no deploy is caught within a day rather than a week. Confirming the diagnosis: replay the failing cases through the fallback provider or a pinned snapshot and compare.

D3. Hypotheses consistent with the facts: (1) the filter is correct but the index metadata is wrong, so the document carries groups: ["retail"] in the source but was indexed with all or with no groups, and the filter admitted it; the trace shows the groups from the source document record, not from the index. (2) The filter is correct and applied, but on a different path: a cache hit returned a result computed for a retail user with the same normalized query, bypassing retrieval entirely. (3) The filter is applied to the primary retrieval but not to a secondary source, such as query expansion, a "related chunks" step, or a parent-document fetch that pulls siblings of an allowed chunk without re-checking their groups. The single additional trace field that distinguishes them: the retrieval-stage provenance per evidence item, for example retrieved_via with values like primary, cache, parent_expand, together with the groups as read from the index at retrieval time. A cache provenance confirms (2), a non-primary provenance confirms (3), and primary provenance with index-time groups differing from source groups confirms (1).

docs.title: Knowledge questions
docs.text:
K1. Any three of the following, each tied to its mechanism. (1) Cost and TTFT: every token in the handbook is processed at prefill on every request, and attention cost grows with the square of the prompt length, so the per-request bill and the time to first token both rise, the latter faster than linearly. (2) Serving memory: every token in context occupies KV cache for the whole request (2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × tokens × bytes), so a 1M-token context per user bounds concurrency to a handful of sessions per accelerator, and a hosted provider's rate limits reflect the same arithmetic. (3) Attention dilution and lost-in-the-middle: recall of a fact depends on its position and on how many distractors compete; a handbook puts most facts in the middle among thousands of irrelevant passages. (4) Trust: attention cannot distinguish instructions from data, so the entire handbook becomes an instruction channel. (5) Evidence: the advertised size is an input limit, not a measured recall at that length on this workload. A retrieval stage that selects a few relevant sections addresses all five.

K2. BPE merges are learned by frequency on the training corpus. Text that was abundant in the corpus (English, common code) accumulates long merges and tokenizes into few pieces; text that was rare (Cyrillic, Azerbaijani diacritics and suffixes) has few merges and falls back toward short pieces or raw bytes. Different vocabularies were trained on different corpora with different sizes, so the penalty differs per vocabulary: the newer one in the experiment charges 42 tokens for the Russian sentence, the older one 80. Before committing to a cost model, the team must (a) identify the exact tokenizer of the model they will ship on, (b) measure token counts on a representative sample of real traffic per language and content type, not on English test strings, (c) express the budget and the price per request per language from those measurements, and (d) re-measure when the model changes.

K3. Total time is 3.8 s + 300 × 0.025 s = 11.3 s, so decode is most of the elapsed time, but the user's wait before seeing anything is the 3.8 s TTFT, which is driven by the 40k-token prompt (prefill, roughly quadratic) plus queueing. Change the prompt first: retrieve or compress to a few thousand relevant tokens, which also cuts cost. Streaming hides the 7.5 s of decode behind visible output but does nothing about the 3.8 s before the first token, which already breaks Northwind's p95 TTFT target of 2 s. A max_tokens cap is the separate lever for the decode phase.

K4. Temperature divides the logits before softmax. It rescales the distribution without changing the ranking: below 1 the mass concentrates on the top candidates, above 1 it spreads toward the tail, and the entropy rises or falls accordingly. Top-p keeps the smallest set of top tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p and renormalizes, so it deletes the tail outright and adapts the surviving set to the model's confidence. At temperature 2 alone, individually absurd tokens each keep around one percent of the mass; over a few hundred steps one of them will almost surely be drawn, so the output derails. Top-p 0.9 removes those tokens entirely while leaving the plausible candidates, now flattened by the temperature, in proportion. The combination gives diversity among reasonable continuations without the tail; temperature alone gives diversity including the tail.

K5. Preference tuning. Pretraining gives no particular reason to accept a premise, and instruction tuning teaches format and task-following. Preference tuning optimizes the model toward answers that raters prefer, and raters (human or model) tend to prefer answers that agree with them, take the request at face value, and sound confident. The model therefore learns to treat the user's framing as given, which is sycophancy: it answers the question that was asked, on the user's false premise, instead of correcting it. Changes outside the model, any two of: (1) ground the answer in retrieved policy text and instruct the model to answer from the evidence and to state when the evidence contradicts the question, so the true carry-over rule is in context and competes with the premise; (2) add an output check that compares claims in the answer (or the accepted premise) against the retrieved evidence and routes contradictions to a correction or abstention path (Chapter 13); (3) add leading-question and false-premise cases to the evaluation set so the rate of premise acceptance is measured on every prompt or model change (Chapter 24); (4) phrase the system contract neutrally rather than with "always help the user do what they ask," which reinforces the learned tendency. Rewording the question is not a fix, because the user controls it.

K6. KV bytes = 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × tokens × bytes_per_element, per sequence; multiply by concurrency for the total. Fixed by the model: layers, kv_heads, head_dim, and (within what the engine supports) bytes_per_element. Fixed by the request: tokens, which is prompt plus output so far, and across requests, concurrency. GQA reduces kv_heads by sharing one key/value head across a group of query heads, so the cache shrinks by the sharing factor and more sequences fit in the same memory. An 8-bit cache format halves bytes_per_element, which halves the cache again, at some quality cost that must be evaluated on long-context tasks.

docs.title: Engineering questions
docs.text:
E1. Candidate changes: (1) compact the schema: strip indentation and whitespace, shorten descriptions to the minimum that still steers the model, remove redundant title and example fields, and collapse repeated sub-objects into $ref definitions if the provider's constrained decoder accepts them; (2) when the provider enforces the schema server-side, stop also describing it in the prompt text, and measure whether the native mode bills the schema as input tokens (providers differ), or use provider prompt caching so the fixed schema prefix is billed at the cached rate (Chapter 5); (3) split the schema: a small routing call decides which of several narrow schemas applies, and only that one is sent. Measurement: record usage.input_tokens per request before and after from the provider's usage field, not an estimate, and compute the delta on a replay of a week of real tickets. Quality: run the existing extraction evaluation set (field-level precision and recall against labeled tickets) on both configurations with identical sampling settings and at least a few hundred cases, and require no statistically meaningful drop on any field. Ship behind a flag and compare the two arms on production traffic for a day before switching fully.

E2. Replace string equality with layered contract assertions. (1) Structural: the output parses and validates against the pydantic schema; catches truncation, malformed JSON, missing fields. (2) Field-level: each extracted field equals the labeled value after normalization (dates to ISO, amounts to Decimal, strings trimmed and case-folded); catches wrong values while ignoring formatting variance. (3) Set-valued or tolerant assertions where several answers are acceptable: category in an allowed set, free-text summary passes a rubric check or a judge with a fixed prompt (Chapter 24); catches semantic drift without demanding one wording. (4) Repeat each case N times at the deployed settings and require that structural and field-level assertions pass every time, which turns nondeterminism into a measured flake rate instead of a surprise. (5) Pin the model identifier and sampling configuration in the test fixture and record them with every result, so a provider-side model change shows up as a labeled regression rather than as random failures. The string-equality assertion is kept only against the response cache, where bit-exact repeats are expected because the model is skipped.

E3. Per token: A: 2 × 40 × 32 × 128 × 2 = 655,360 bytes (640 KiB); B: 2 × 48 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 196,608 bytes (192 KiB). At 24,000 tokens: A ≈ 14.65 GiB per sequence, B ≈ 4.39 GiB. Eight concurrent sessions: A ≈ 117 GiB, B ≈ 35 GiB. Only B fits in 60 GiB; A would fit about four sessions at that context length, or needs an 8-bit cache (≈ 59 GiB, borderline) or shorter contexts. Before deciding you also need: weight memory for each model at the serving precision (it comes out of the same device memory before any KV budget exists); measured quality on your own evaluation set at your context lengths, because "similar quality" is a benchmark claim; TPOT and TTFT under load, since B's extra layers cost per-step compute and memory traffic; engine support for the cache format and for GQA kernels; and license and operational constraints.

E4. Mechanism: a reasoning model decodes a stretch of thinking tokens before the visible answer; each is a sequential decode step, occupies KV cache, and is usually billed as output. Predictions by workload. Ticket triage: a short prompt and a one-word label; thinking adds hundreds to thousands of decode steps to an answer that needed a handful, so time to the visible answer rises from well under a second to seconds, cost per request rises by an order of magnitude, and accuracy barely moves because classification is not multi-step. Policy questions: the prompt is long, so TTFT was already prefill-dominated; thinking adds decode time on top, cost rises several times, and quality gains are small because the answer is a lookup in retrieved evidence; KV occupancy per request grows with prompt plus thinking tokens and is held longer, so fewer requests fit at once on a self-hosted engine (and provider rate limits on output tokens are hit sooner). Invoice reconciliation: the one workload with genuine multi-step structure, so this is where quality can improve, but arithmetic should still go to a calculator tool. Across all three, cost per request becomes highly variable, because thinking length varies by request, which makes budgets and per-tenant forecasts harder. Under an unchanged max_tokens sized for visible answers, thinking consumes the budget and the length finish rate rises, most visibly on reconciliation and on structured outputs, where truncation means unparseable JSON. Test first: the length rate and output-token distribution on a replay of a few hundred real requests per workload at the proposed effort, because it is cheap, it breaks correctness immediately if wrong, and the same replay yields measured time-to-visible-answer and cost per request; then compare quality per workload against the current model on the evaluation set. The expected conclusion is to enable high effort only for the reconciliation route, which is what Chapter 7's router does.

docs.title: Practical exercises
docs.text:
P1. Expected implementation: a --file PATH argument; a split_sections(markdown) -> list[tuple[str, str]] that splits on lines matching ^#{1,6}\s and keeps the preamble as its own section; per-section count_tokens with the same TokenCount provenance; a table with section title, tokens, and share of the total; a final row for the whole document. Acceptance: the test builds a synthetic document of three headed sections, asserts the section list has the expected titles in order, asserts the sum of per-section counts equals the count of the whole document under the heuristic (which is additive) and is within a small tolerance under the real tokenizer (BPE is not strictly additive at boundaries, so assert abs(sum - whole) <= number_of_sections), and runs offline by passing an invalid encoding name to force the heuristic path. The script must still print the original sample table when --file is absent.

P2. Expected implementation: repetition_penalty(logits, generated_ids, penalty) returns a copy of the logits where, for each index in generated_ids, a positive logit is divided by penalty and a negative logit is multiplied by penalty (penalty > 1 reduces the chance of repeating; penalty == 1 is the identity). sample gains an optional generated_ids and repetition_penalty pair applied before temperature. Tests: identity at penalty 1; probability of every generated token strictly decreases and of non-generated tokens increases after softmax for penalty 1.5; the function does not mutate its input; indices out of range raise. Demo: a toy vocabulary for a code line such as total = total + item where total legitimately appears twice; show that after the first total is generated, a penalty of 1.5 to 2.0 pushes the second occurrence below an alternative identifier, producing wrong code. The written conclusion is that stop sequences and length caps are safer first responses to loops in code generation.

P3. Expected implementation: build_context(paragraphs, fact, position) that returns a list of Message objects (system contract, a long user message of filler paragraphs with the fact inserted at the given fractional position, and the question); a run_sweep(client, positions) -> list[SweepResult] recording position, context tokens via count_tokens, and whether the answer contained the expected value; and a Markdown table renderer. With FakeLLM(handler=...) the handler can be scripted to answer correctly only when the fact lies within the first or last 20 percent of the user message, which lets the tests exercise the whole harness and produce a visibly U-shaped table. Acceptance: tests assert the fact is present exactly once at the requested position, that token counts grow monotonically with the number of filler paragraphs, that the result table has one row per position, and that swapping the fake for any LLMClient requires no code change. The README note states that the real curve must be measured per model and context length.

P4. Expected implementation: --sweep-tokens 4000,16000,64000,128000 (comma-separated) prints, for each length, per-sequence cache, bytes per token (constant), and maximum concurrent sequences under --memory-gb; without a budget it prints only the per-sequence sizes. Acceptance: test that per-sequence bytes are strictly increasing with tokens, that maximum concurrency is non-increasing, that the 128k row equals eight times the 16k row, and that the CLI exits non-zero with a clear message when the list contains a non-integer or a negative value.

docs.title: Debugging exercises
docs.text:
D1. Root cause: the new model tokenizes the same JSON output into more tokens than the old one (a different vocabulary, or a tendency to emit more verbose output such as extra whitespace, longer string values, or added fields), so the same max_tokens = 400 now truncates the tail of the object. The telemetry confirms it: every failure has finish_reason = "length", the inputs did not change, and the output token count on failing requests sits exactly at the cap. Fixes to consider: raise max_tokens to the measured p99 output length of the new model plus margin, and treat length as a failure that triggers a repair or retry rather than a parse attempt; or reduce output size by compacting the schema (no indentation, shorter keys, fewer optional fields) and by using constrained decoding so no prose surrounds the object. Either way, add a regression test that asserts a natural stop on the longest realistic ticket, and re-run the token-budget test on every model change.

D2. Diagnosis path: the client-side check uses chars / 4, which is calibrated for English; Georgian script costs several times more tokens per character with most vocabularies, so a conversation that passes the character check can exceed the real token limit by a factor of two or more. Telemetry: compare usage.input_tokens from the provider (exact) against the client's estimate per request and group by detected language; the Georgian group shows a tokens-per-character ratio far above 0.25 while the English group sits near it. Requests that failed show the exact count above the limit while the estimate was below it. The counter provenance field, if the server uses the Chapter 2 pattern, will read heuristic on the failing path. Fix: count with the model's real tokenizer (or the provider's count endpoint) in the context builder, enforce the budget on the exact count, and add a language-stratified budget test. The deeper lesson is that the heuristic should have been labeled and alerted on, not trusted silently.

D3. Saturated resource: KV-cache memory on the accelerator, not compute. Long pasted documents multiply tokens per session; at 128 KiB per token for a mid-sized model (the chapter's illustrative configuration), a 50k-token session holds about 6 GiB of cache, so a few dozen such sessions exhaust the cache that comfortably held 40 short chats. New requests wait for cache blocks to free up, which shows as queueing with modest GPU utilization, because decode is memory-bound and the engine is now admission-limited. Confirmation: the engine's KV-cache utilization metric near 100%, number of waiting versus running sequences rising together, preemption or swap counters incrementing, and the arithmetic free_memory / (bytes_per_token × p95_context_tokens) matching the observed concurrency cliff. Mitigations with trade-offs: (1) cap context per request and route long documents through retrieval or summarization before the model, which lowers memory and TTFT at the cost of a pipeline and some recall; (2) switch to an 8-bit KV cache or a model with fewer key/value heads, which doubles or quadruples capacity at a small quality cost that must be evaluated on long-context tasks; (3) add admission control and a separate queue or pool for long-context requests so short chats keep their latency, at the cost of longer waits for the heavy requests; (4) add hardware, which is the most expensive and does not fix the underlying unbounded context policy.

docs.title: Knowledge questions
docs.text:
K1. The provider validates that every tool message answers a tool call that appears in the immediately preceding assistant turn. The assistant message with tool_calls is that turn: it carries the ids the results reference and the model's own text, which the next generation step conditions on. Omitting it produces an invalid request (an InvalidRequestError, typically a 400 complaining about an unmatched tool_call_id) in the OpenAI dialect, and in the Anthropic dialect a tool_result block with no matching tool_use block. Even on a lenient server, dropping the assistant turn deletes the model's reasoning about why it called the tool, which degrades the final answer.

K2. Where it lives: the exact-match response cache lives in your process or your Redis; provider prompt caching lives inside the provider's inference stack. Key: the response cache is keyed by a hash of the whole request (model, messages, tools, schema, temperature, max tokens, stop); prompt caching is keyed by an exact prefix of the token sequence the provider has recently computed. What it saves: the response cache saves the entire call, so latency is near zero and cost is zero on a hit (the gateway records the price it would have paid as avoided_cost_usd, separate from cost_usd); prompt caching saves part of the prefill compute, so the call still happens, output tokens are still generated and billed, and cached input tokens are billed at a reduced rate. The response cache is only safe for deterministic requests; prompt caching is always safe because the output is still freshly generated.

K3. At most three attempts, by max_attempts. It may make fewer because of the deadline. After attempt one the delay is uniform in [0, 0.5]; after attempt two it is uniform in [0, 1.0]. The gateway checks _fits(delay, deadline) before sleeping: if elapsed time plus the drawn delay reaches two seconds, it stops retrying that client and moves to the next one (or gives up with a TimeoutError whose cause is the last 503). Since each attempt also consumes real time at the provider, a slow 503 (say 1.2 seconds) plus a drawn delay of 0.9 would already exceed the deadline after attempt two.

K4. Fallback is triggered by the retryable classes: RateLimitError, TimeoutError, and ProviderUnavailableError. These describe the provider's state, so another provider may well succeed. InvalidRequestError describes your request; another provider will reject it too, or worse, accept something you did not mean. ContentFilterError is a policy decision about the content; routing around it is both futile and a governance problem. MalformedResponseError is excluded because the HTTP call succeeded and the problem is the generated content; the right remedy is the structured-output repair loop (re-ask with the error), not a transport retry or a different vendor, and a retry at the gateway level would hide the fact that the model is producing unusable output.

K5. A text fragment is useful on its own: a reader can start reading, and concatenation is lossless. A tool-call argument fragment is a slice of a JSON string that cannot be parsed, validated against the tool's schema, or authorized until the closing brace arrives; emitting it would push every consumer to implement incremental JSON parsing and defer validation. Nothing useful can be done with half a tool call, so the adapter buffers fragments per call index and emits one complete, parsed ToolCall when the stream closes the call. The cost is that tool execution cannot begin until the call is fully described, which for millisecond tools is negligible.

K6. Streaming reduces the user's perceived wait: the time until text first appears on screen. Without streaming, that wait equals the whole generation time; with streaming it drops to roughly the server-side time to first token (TTFT), which governs whether the interface feels responsive. Server-side TTFT itself (queueing plus prefill, Chapter 2) is unchanged; only prompt size and load move it. Total completion time (TTFT plus time per output token times output length) governs how long until the answer is complete and usable, and, for structured outputs, when parsing can start; streaming does not change it either, and max_tokens is the lever that bounds it. Northwind's targets separate the two server-side numbers for exactly this reason: p95 TTFT under two seconds, which is the user's perceived wait only because answers are streamed, and p95 completion under eight.

K7. Empty answers: a reasoning model generates hidden thinking tokens before the visible answer, and on most APIs those count against max_tokens. On harder tickets the thinking alone uses up the 150-token budget, so generation stops with finish_reason length before any visible token is produced; Completion.truncated is true, and complete_structured raises TruncatedOutputError rather than repairing. Bill: thinking tokens are billed as output tokens at the output rate, which is typically several times the input rate, so each request now pays for hundreds of invisible output tokens; the price per token is not the right comparison, cost per completed task is. The spans show it as a jump and a long tail in output_tokens with unchanged visible answer length. Fixes: raise max_tokens to cover thinking plus answer (measured from the output_tokens distribution, for example its p99), and use the provider's reasoning-effort or thinking-budget setting to cap thinking for a task this simple; or route the classifier back to a non-reasoning model if the evaluation set shows no accuracy gain, which is the usual outcome for short classification. Add an alert on the length share so the next model change cannot reintroduce the problem silently.

docs.title: Engineering questions
docs.text:
E1. Bug: the cache key is a hash of the request content. If two tenants send identical prompts (same system prompt, same question) and permission is enforced in the tool layer rather than reflected in the prompt, the second tenant receives the first tenant's cached completion, including any tool calls or data the first tenant's request legitimately produced. That is a cross-tenant leak, which violates the zero-leakage target.

Fix A, identity in the key: set metadata["cache_scope"] to the tenant (and the user id where personalization matters) on every request; it is the one metadata field the gateway's cache_key includes. Construct the shared gateway with require_cache_scope=True so a request that arrives without a scope is never cached. Simple, no prompt changes, keeps hit rates within a tenant. Cost: the scope must be set by the request-handling layer from the authenticated identity, never from model or user input, and hit rates drop roughly by the number of scopes. A test sends two identical requests with different scopes and asserts two provider calls.

Fix B, identity in the prompt: put the tenant and permission scope into the system prompt (Tenant: retail. Allowed tools: ...). The existing key now differs automatically. Cost: the system prompt is no longer a stable shared prefix across tenants, so provider prompt-cache hit rates fall, and permission text in the prompt is advisory to the model, so the tool layer must still enforce it.

Tradeoff: A is the engineering fix (explicit, testable, no prompt coupling); B also gives the model useful context but spends prompt-cache efficiency and tempts people to treat the prompt as the enforcement point. Most systems do A, and add B only where the model needs to know the tenant to answer well.

E2. Illustrative numbers; the method matters. Suppose the provider allows 500 requests per minute and 400,000 tokens per minute, and each ticket is about 600 input tokens with a 100-token structured answer.

  • Rate limiter: RateLimiter(requests_per_minute=450, tokens_per_minute=360_000), about ten percent under the published limits, because the token estimate counts the full max_tokens and other services may share the key. Set max_tokens=150 so the estimate (600 + 150) is tight; the token bucket then admits about 480 requests per minute, so the request bucket is the binding constraint.
  • Concurrency: with a two-second typical latency, 450 requests per minute needs about 15 in flight; max_concurrency=24 leaves headroom for tail latency without flooding.
  • Cache: enable the exact-match cache. Tickets repeat (automated alerts, duplicate submissions) and temperature is zero; a hit rate of even ten percent is five thousand free calls.
  • Retries: RetryPolicy(max_attempts=4, base_delay_s=1.0, max_delay_s=30.0, jitter=True). A batch job can afford longer backoff; the limiter already prevents self-inflicted 429s.
  • Timeout: timeout_s=60 per ticket; a nightly job prefers completing over being fast.
  • Fallback: a second model on the same provider or a second provider, but only after running the evaluation set against it, because classification labels drift between models.
  • Alternative: if the provider has a batch API, submit the whole night's work there at the discount and skip the limiter entirely; keep the gateway path for the daytime trickle.

E3. Implement stream as a thin emulation over complete: call complete, then yield one text_delta with the whole text, one tool_call_delta per tool call, a usage event, and done with the real finish reason. This satisfies the protocol and keeps callers working. Do not lie about latency: do not chunk the text and sleep between chunks to fake typing, because TTFT would then be total latency plus artificial delay, and the span would misrepresent the provider. Set a class attribute such as supports_streaming = False so that UIs can choose to show a spinner instead of a cursor, and record stream=False on the span even when called through stream. The done event should carry the finish reason exactly as complete would have returned it; usage should carry the real usage so cost accounting is unchanged.

E4. Key: the embedding of a normalized form of the request (system prompt version id, tool set hash, and the user text), stored alongside the exact-match hash so exact hits still short-circuit. Threshold policy: a cosine similarity threshold per task class, not global; classification and FAQ-style questions tolerate a higher threshold than open questions, and any request with tools or a response schema should require an exact match on the schema and tool set plus the similarity threshold on text. Invalidation: flush on prompt version change, model change, or embedding model change; TTL by task; and never serve a semantic hit across tenants. Evaluation before enabling: take a sample of production request pairs that would have been served as hits at the candidate threshold, generate fresh answers for the second request, and have a judge (Chapter 24) grade whether the cached answer would have been acceptable; plot the false-hit rate against the threshold, pick the threshold where false hits are below your tolerance, and measure the resulting hit rate to see whether the saving justifies the new failure mode.

docs.title: Practical exercises
docs.text:
P1. IdempotentGateway. Expected implementation: a wrapper holding inner: LLMClient, a lock, a dict of completed results keyed by idempotency key, and a dict of in-flight threading.Event (or asyncio.Future) objects. complete reads req.metadata.get("idempotency_key"); with no key it delegates. With a key, under the lock it returns a stored result, or if another call is in flight waits on its event and then returns the stored result, or otherwise registers itself as in flight, releases the lock, calls inner.complete, stores the result, and sets the event. Failures must also be stored (or the in-flight marker cleared) so waiters do not hang. Acceptance: eight threads calling with the same key against a FakeLLM produce exactly one entry in fake.requests and eight identical completions; a scripted ProviderUnavailableError on the first call does not deadlock the waiters; different keys produce different calls; an optional TTL evicts completed entries.

P2. Streaming tool loop. Expected implementation: a loop with a step limit; each iteration calls client.stream(req), prints text deltas as they arrive, collects tool_call_delta events, and on done appends an assistant Message reconstructed from the text and tool calls (use collect_stream). If there are tool calls, execute each against a dict of callables, append Message.tool(call.id, json.dumps(result)), and continue; otherwise return. Script FakeLLM(handler=...) so the first request (no tool results in messages) returns a lookup_employee call, the second (which contains a tool message) returns search_tickets, and the third returns final text. Acceptance: three requests recorded; the second request's last two messages are the assistant turn with the tool call and the tool result with the matching id; the loop stops on the step limit when the handler always returns a tool call; a ContentFilterError from the stream propagates rather than being retried.

P3. RedisResponseCache. Expected implementation: a class with get/set matching the ResponseCache protocol, serializing with completion.model_dump_json() and Completion.model_validate_json, using SET key value EX ttl when a TTL is given. Provide a FakeRedis with get, set(ex=...), and a manual clock so TTL expiry is testable. Acceptance: a parametrized test runs the same gateway scenarios (hit, miss, TTL expiry, no caching at temperature 0.8) against InMemoryResponseCache and RedisResponseCache(FakeRedis()) and both pass; a serialization round trip preserves usage, tool_calls, and raw; the gateway's cache_hit annotation is true on the second call with either cache.

P4. PrefixStabilityCheck. Expected implementation: a helper assert_stable_prefix(render, min_bytes) that renders the prompt for two requests with different user content and asserts rendered_a[:min_bytes] == rendered_b[:min_bytes], reporting the first differing offset and a few bytes of context on failure. Apply it to a Northwind system prompt that opens with Today is {date}; the test fails with the offset pointing at the date. Fix by moving the date (and anything else volatile, such as the user's name or tenant) after the stable instructions and tool definitions, or into the first user message. Acceptance: the test fails on the original prompt and passes on the fixed one; a second test asserts the prompt still contains the date somewhere so the fix did not simply delete it.

docs.title: Debugging exercises
docs.text:
D1. Candidate causes and the evidence for each:

  1. The request's timeout_s is not reaching the gateway. A middle layer builds a new CompletionRequest and drops the field, so the gateway uses its 60-second default. Confirm: the first attempt's span should carry the request timeout; log attempt_req.timeout_s or check the HTTP request's read timeout, which would show 60 instead of 10.
  2. Retry-After hints are large and the deadline check is being bypassed. The 429s carry retry-after: 15, and the policy honors the hint. The gateway's _fits should refuse a 15-second sleep against a 10-second budget, so if sleeps happened, either the budget was 60 (cause 1) or a custom RetryPolicy subclass overrode delay_for without the deadline check. Confirm: the retry_after_s attribute on the recorded exceptions and the gaps between span start times (about 15 seconds apart would match the hint).
  3. The rate limiter is sleeping outside the deadline check. A limiter constructed with the real sleep but without passing deadline (a custom admission wrapper) can block indefinitely before the span even opens. Confirm: queue_ms on the spans; a large queue_ms on attempt one points at the limiter, not at retries.
  4. Provider A is slow to return 429. Each 429 took several seconds; three attempts plus two backoffs add up. Confirm: latency_ms on the error spans (should be near zero for a real 429) versus span duration.

The single most informative attribute is the first span's effective timeout; the second is the gap between consecutive span start times.

D2. The deploy made the system prompt's leading bytes volatile. Typical culprits: a timestamp or date inserted at the top (Today is 2026-...), a request or session id, the user's name, or reordering so that a per-request section (retrieved documents, user profile) now precedes the shared instructions. Provider prompt caching keys on an exact token prefix; a byte that changes per request breaks the prefix for every call, so cached_input_tokens collapses and every input token is billed at the full rate. Thirty-five percent is consistent with a long system prompt and tool list that previously hit the cache on most requests. The test that would have caught it is the prefix-stability check from P4 (render the prompt twice with different user content and assert the first N bytes are identical), run in CI on every prompt change, plus an alert on the cached_input_tokens / input_tokens ratio in production.

D3. The symptoms exclude the obvious causes: finish_reason="stop" with low output_tokens means the provider believes it finished, not that it hit max_tokens, and no error events means the adapter did not see a stream error. The gateway span is ok, so the semaphore and relay completed normally. Two places remain. First, upstream of the gateway: the application's own SSE or WebSocket layer to the browser may be dropping the final chunks when the client's buffer flushes late, or an intermediate proxy buffers and truncates streams at a size or time boundary; in that case the gateway saw the whole answer and the user did not. Second, downstream: a stop sequence in the request (stop=[...]) that the model legitimately hits mid-sentence, for example a stop string like \n\n or ### that also appears in normal prose; the provider reports stop and a short answer, which is exactly this signature at a low rate.

Experiments: (1) Compare the text reconstructed from the gateway's events (log collect_stream output, or the final text length, on the span) with what the browser rendered for an affected request; if they match, the truncation is in generation (check the stop list); if the gateway has more text than the browser, the loss is in your delivery path or a proxy. (2) Replay the affected request's messages with the same stop list against complete instead of stream; if the answer is truncated identically, it is the stop sequence, and removing or tightening the stop list fixes it.

docs.title: Chapter 4 — Solutions: Prompt Engineering as Engineering
docs.text: Identifiers match the exercises in book/chapters/04-prompt-engineering.md.

docs.title: Knowledge questions
docs.text:
K1. Role: without it (when it matters) the model picks its own register, for example adding friendly prose to output that software parses. Task: without a single imperative statement of what to produce, output varies in kind, not just in quality. Constraints: without category definitions, ordered rules, and limits, borderline inputs are decided inconsistently and outputs drift in length and content. Evidence, labeled and separated: without it the model answers from its parametric memory, and without labels it may treat retrieved text as instructions or fail to cite. Output schema: without it parsers break on prose, missing fields, or invented fields; the prompt states the schema and a validator enforces it. Failure behavior: without an explicit other, abstain flag, or empty-citation branch, the model produces a plausible answer when it should decline, which is the root of many hallucination incidents. (The decoding policy is a seventh element of the contract in this chapter's files, versioned in the front matter.)

K2. System instructions carry deployment policy, developer instructions carry task guidance (folded into the system role in aie_core), user messages carry the request, and data (documents, tool results, files) carries material with no authority. Models are trained to prefer higher levels when they conflict, so placing each kind of text at the right level makes correct behavior the path of least resistance: format and refusal rules in the system message hold even when a user asks otherwise, and a labeled document's embedded request is usually ignored. It is not a boundary because it is a learned tendency of a probabilistic reader, not an enforced rule: persuasive user text or document text can still win. Anything an attacker would want, such as tool authority, data access, or secrets, must be controlled by code outside the model (Chapter 26).

K3. Both change behavior. Temperature and token limits change the output distribution; the schema changes what the model is asked to produce and what the validator accepts (and, with provider structured output, what decoding allows). If they were outside the hash, a trace saying ticket.classify@1.1.0 could refer to two different behaviors. Example incident: someone lowers maxLength of evidence from 200 to 50 in the shared schema; schema-valid rate drops because longer quotes now fail validation, but every trace still shows 1.1.0 with an unchanged hash, so on-call engineers search the prompt text and the model for a change that is not there.

K4. Free-form reasoning is prose the model writes before answering; it may improve accuracy on multi-step tasks but costs output tokens and proves nothing, since a fluent rationale can accompany a wrong answer. Verifiable artifacts are structured intermediate outputs that code can check. Router: (1) an evidence field that must be an exact quote from the ticket, checked by normalized substring match against the input (quote_in_variable); (2) a matched_rule index naming which decision rule applied, checked by verifying the rule's keywords occur in the ticket and no earlier rule matches. Answering prompt: citations as document ids, checked as a subset of the ids actually provided in the request; a stronger version adds one supporting quote per citation, checked as a substring of that document's text.

K5. Tokens on every request (prefill latency and input cost; the chapter's 1.1.0 grew input about fourfold); surface bias (outputs imitate example length, labels, phrasing); leakage (examples overlapping test cases inflate scores); spurious correlations (a feature shared by examples of one label becomes a shortcut). Measure by ablation: run the full suite with and without the example at fixed settings, with repeats if temperature is above zero, and compare per-case fixes and regressions and the token delta. Keep the example only if it fixes cases it was meant for without regressing others and the token cost is acceptable.

K6. HTML escaping converts <, >, &, and quotes into entities everywhere, which corrupts code, emails, and logs, while the model reads the entities as roughly the same characters anyway, so nothing is protected. Correct escaping for untrusted prompt variables: render the value inside an explicit labeled delimiter; neutralize any occurrence of the delimiter inside the value so it cannot close its own block or open a new one; normalize look-alike characters (NFKC) before that check; drop control and invisible formatting characters such as zero-width spaces and bidirectional overrides; optionally cap length per variable. Separately, never build template source from untrusted input.

docs.title: Engineering questions
docs.text:
E1. Minimum guarantees: (1) Immutable versions: every save creates a new version with a monotonically assigned number; published versions cannot be edited, only superseded. (2) Content hash per version, covering text, decoding policy, and schema, returned by the read API and stored in an append-only history. (3) Separate draft and served states: drafts are editable and unservable; serving happens only through named aliases (prod, canary) whose changes are audited with author, time, and reason. (4) A promotion gate: moving an alias runs the regression suite for that prompt against the candidate and stores the report; promotion is blocked on gate failure unless an authorized override with a reason is recorded. (5) Trace identity: the runtime client returns id, version, and hash with every rendered prompt and the application records them on spans and request metadata. (6) Rollback: alias changes are reversible in one action and the runtime picks them up within a bounded time (cache TTL). (7) Schema and variable declarations are validated on save (undeclared variables, taint rules) so the UI cannot produce a prompt that fails at render time. (8) Exportable history so incidents can be replayed with the exact version. Without 1 to 5, the UI reintroduces silent drift and the attribution problem.

E2. Plan: (1) Freeze prompt changes for the twelve prompts for the duration of the migration, so only one variable changes. (2) For each prompt, run its suite with repeats against the current model (fresh baseline, since provider behavior can drift) and against the new model at the same prompt version and decoding policy. (3) Classify: prompts with no regressions and acceptable cost and latency are migrated first; prompts with regressions get new minor versions tuned for the new model, evaluated against the new model, and paired explicitly (a model hint or a routing rule that serves version N+1 only on the new model). (4) Canary per prompt: route a traffic slice to the new model with the paired version, with dashboards sliced by model and prompt.version, compare schema-valid rate, distribution metrics, downstream signals, TTFT, and tokens. (5) Promote prompt by prompt, keeping the old model and old versions available for rollback. Attribution is preserved because at each step exactly one of {model, prompt version} differs between compared arms; when both must change for a prompt, first measure the model change alone on the old version, then the prompt change alone on the new model, so each delta is known.

E3. System message, stable and first: role, task, constraints, citation rules, data-labeling statement, output schema, failure behavior, and a fixed sentence such as "Answer in the language specified in the request" so the policy itself is stable. User message, after the stable prefix: the documents as labeled data blocks, then the per-request language code as a trusted variable (it comes from the user's profile or the request header your code validated against an allowlist of language codes), then the question as untrusted data. Rationale: the language instruction is per-request, so putting its value into the system message would make the prefix differ by language and fragment the cache; keeping a fixed instruction in the system message preserves the hierarchy (the rule is policy) while the value is request data. Documents go before the question so the question sits closest to the point of generation; if documents are shared across many requests (for example a fixed policy pack), they can move into the stable prefix to be cached, but per-request retrieved documents cannot. A user asking in the question to "ignore the language setting" is untrusted data and does not override the system rule.

E4. Gate: block on any regression among critical cases; block on a net pass-rate drop beyond a small tolerance; treat other regressions as review items rather than blockers; never count errored cases as regressions. Suite changes: run each case three to five times and define a case's status by its pass rate, so a flaky case is reported as flaky rather than flipping between passing and failing across runs; mark persistently flaky cases and investigate whether the label is ambiguous, the prompt is underspecified, or the case needs temperature 0; grow the suite (40 cases makes each case worth 2.5 points) toward a size where aggregate changes mean something (Chapter 24); split cases by tag so the report shows which category moved. Require that any override of the gate records a reason in the pull request. This keeps real regressions on important cases blocking while removing noise that trains engineers to ignore the gate.

E5. Router: not now. Seventeen cases is a smoke test, one case is about six points of pass rate, and an optimizer searching against it will find wording that fits these tickets, not the traffic. The error analysis also says part of the remaining failures are a label question (TCK-2026-0043) that no wording fixes. First grow the suite from production traffic to a few hundred labeled tickets, fix ambiguous labels, and split off a held-out set the optimizer never scores against. Answer prompt: closer, because each dimension already has a deterministic assertion, but 24 cases is still small, and the content dimension is exactly the one an optimizer will trade away for length and format unless contains assertions on key facts and conditions are weighted as critical. Adopt it once the suite is a few hundred cases with a held-out split, the metric combines all dimensions with critical content checks as hard constraints, and any judge in the metric is calibrated (Chapter 24). Release process for both: the optimizer's best prompt becomes a draft file with a new version number; a human reviews it for odd rules, leaked test content, or instructions that weaken the data-labeling statement; it runs through compare against prod on the held-out set and the normal gate (critical regressions, token budget); it is locked, served on the canary alias, and promoted like any hand-written version. Run the model upgrade first with unchanged prompts, so the optimizer's gain is measured against the new model alone and attribution is preserved.

docs.title: Practical exercises
docs.text:
P1. Expected solution: copy 1.2.0.md to 1.3.0.md, set version = "1.3.0", and make two edits to the decision rules: remove the ambiguous keyword "till" from the payments rule (it matches "still"), and add a rule "- If the ticket mentions stolen, choose hardware." after the payments rule and before the account and password rules, so "The laptop was locked" no longer routes a theft report to password support. With the simulated router this fixes TCK-2026-0007 and TCK-2026-0023 with no regressions (pass rate 16 of 17; TCK-2026-0043 remains, a label question). Set status = "active" when done and run prompts_cli.py lock; verify must report no problems and the lock must gain ticket.classify@1.3.0. New cases: one ticket whose text contains a common word containing a short keyword (for example "We still cannot print labels" with gold warehouse_scanner or the right category for the content), and one theft or loss report that also mentions "locked" or "password" (for example "Phone stolen on the train, it was locked with my password"), both tagged with their categories and the theft case tagged critical. Acceptance: compare --baseline 1.2.0 --candidate 1.3.0 passes the gate, and both new cases fail on 1.2.0 and pass on 1.3.0.

P2. Expected implementation: Comparison gains regressions_by_tag: dict[str, list[str]], filled in compare from the candidate's case tags. gate(..., max_regressions_by_tag: Mapping[str, int] | None = None) appends a reason for each tag whose regression count exceeds its limit ("pos_payments: 2 regressions (allowed 1)"). render_report adds a section listing per-tag counts for tags with at least one regression. Tests: a synthetic baseline and candidate built with FakeLLM scripted outputs where two pos_payments cases regress and none critical; assert the gate fails with {"pos_payments": 1}, passes with {"pos_payments": 2}, and that the report contains the per-tag line. Existing tests must still pass because the new parameter defaults to None.

P3. Expected implementation: VariableSpec gains marking: Literal["none", "datamark"] = "none" and Untrusted carries it. In Untrusted.escaped, after sanitizing and truncating, if marking is datamark, replace each run of whitespace except newlines with a marker character such as ^ (configurable), and add marking="datamark" to the block attributes so the system prompt can explain the marking. Sanitization and delimiter escaping run before marking, so a forged tag is escaped first. Tests: a value "pay the invoice now" renders as "pay^the^invoice^now" inside the block with the attribute present; a value containing </untrusted_data> still yields exactly one real closing tag; for the router suite with ticket_body marked, the system and example messages are byte-identical across all cases (prefix stability), since marking only affects the final user message. The chapter's static taint check needs no change.

P4. Expected implementation: assist.answer@1.1.0 with schema change (minor if the new field is optional, major if required; choose major and update callers if you make it required): citations becomes a list of objects {"id": str, "quote": str}; the system prompt asks for one short verbatim supporting quote per cited document. New assertion type quotes_in_cited_documents with path pointing at the citations list and variable naming the documents variable: for each citation, find the document with that id in the case variables (fail if absent) and check the normalized quote is a substring of the normalized document text. Cases with scripted FakeLLM outputs: correct quote from the cited document passes; a real quote attributed to the wrong document fails with a message naming the citation; an invented quote fails. The existing subset assertion becomes a check on citations.*.id, or is implemented inside the new assertion. Lock updated; the 1.0.0 answer suite is unchanged.

docs.title: Debugging exercises
docs.text:
D1. Root cause: the new line puts a per-day value into the system section, near the top. Prefix caching requires a byte-identical prefix; everything after the first changing token is no longer cacheable, so almost the entire prompt is recomputed on every request (and the cache fragments by day at best, by request if the value includes time). Quality is unchanged because the model sees the same content; only latency and cost moved. Telemetry: cached input tokens per request (from provider usage, recorded by the gateway as cached_input_tokens) drop to near zero at the deploy; TTFT p50 and p95 step up; both changes align exactly with prompt.version changing from 1.1.0 to 1.2.0 in traces; input token counts are almost unchanged. Fix: move the date into the user message after the stable content (or into a final short system note placed after the static part if your provider allows it), keeping the system section static; release as 1.2.1 or 1.3.0. Test: the prefix-stability test, rendering the prompt with two different today values and asserting all messages before the request-specific user message are identical; it would have failed in CI.

D2. Explanations, most to least likely: (1) The CI suite ran with LLM_PROVIDER=fake, so the behavioral gate exercised the harness and the simulated router, not the real model; nothing tested how the real model ranks the payments and security rules. Evidence: CI configuration and the report header ("using the simulated router"); rerunning the suite against the real provider. (2) Coverage gap: the golden set has no data-exposure ticket worded like the production ones (for example mentioning card numbers), so no critical case regressed even against the real model. Evidence: compare the two production tickets with the suite's critical cases; add them and rerun 1.0.0 and 1.1.0. (3) Nondeterminism: the critical cases pass on one run but not always; the suite used repeats=1. Evidence: rerun with repeats and look for flaky cases. (4) A caller override, such as a higher temperature passed at the call site. Evidence: prompt.overrides in request metadata and the temperature attribute on the prompt.call span for those two requests. (5) Unlikely given the controls: the served file differs from the tested one. Evidence: compare prompt.hash on the production spans with the lock entry for 1.1.0; a match rules this out. Remediation: add both tickets as critical cases, run behavioral suites against the real model with repeats before promotion, and use the canary alias with a security-category distribution monitor.

D3. Likely causes: the judge changed while the answers did not. Candidates: the judge.groundedness prompt was promoted to a new version (for example a rubric edit that made 3 easier to reach), the judge's model changed (a provider upgrade behind an unpinned model name or a router change that sends judge traffic to another model), or the judge's decoding policy was overridden. Check: prompt.version and prompt.hash on the judge's prompt.call spans before and after the jump; model and provider on the judge's llm.complete spans; prompt.overrides in metadata; the registry history and aliases.toml for judge.groundedness; whether the answer prompt's version and model stayed constant (they did, per the scenario). Confirm with the human-labeled calibration set: rerun it with the old and new judge configuration and compare agreement. Prevention: treat the judge like any prompt with an immutable version and pinned model; freeze judge version and model for the duration of any comparison; require a calibration run against human labels before a judge change is promoted; and record judge version and model with every score so dashboards never mix judge configurations.

D4. Root cause: in 1.4.0 the ticket_subject variable was declared trusted = true (or its declaration was dropped and re-added as trusted during the "cleanup"). The trace shows it: the body is inside an <untrusted_data> block, the subject is printed bare after Subject:, so the injected sentence reaches the model as text with the same standing as the prompt's own instructions, and the model obeys it. The evidence quote passes quote_in_variable because it really is a quote from the input, which is why the output also looks valid. Why every control passed: the taint check only constrains untrusted variables, so declaring one trusted switches it off by design; the lock proves the served file is the reviewed file, not that the review was right; the regression suite has no injection probe in the subject (INJ-001 targets the body), so no case regressed; the cache numbers are normal because the change was below the stable prefix. Control: trust is a property of where a value comes from, not of the prompt, so make it checkable in code. Keep a per-prompt allowlist of variables that may be trusted (here only tenant, sourced from the authenticated session) in a reviewed policy file or test, and fail CI when any prompt declares another variable trusted; additionally require code-owner review from the security owner for any diff that touches a trusted = line. Test: a structural test that loads every prompt version and asserts {name for name, spec in pv.spec.variables.items() if spec.trusted} <= TRUSTED_ALLOWLIST[pv.spec.id], plus a behavioral injection probe that places the instruction in the subject and is tagged critical. Telemetry that would have flagged it earlier: the benefits_leave share on the store tenant jumping after the 1.4.0 rollout (the category-distribution alert) and outputs whose evidence quote contains imperative text addressed to the model.

docs.title: Chapter 5 — Solutions: Context Engineering
docs.text: Identifiers match the exercises in book/chapters/05-context-engineering.md.

docs.title: Knowledge questions
docs.text:
K1. Money: input tokens per request, split by section from the manifest's used_by_section, multiplied by the pricing table into cost per request (Chapter 30). Prefill latency: time to first token at p95, correlated with prompt tokens. KV memory: on self-hosted serving, KV-cache utilization and the concurrency it allows (Chapter 34). On a hosted API you observe it indirectly through the provider's length limits and the latency of long prompts. Attention: answer accuracy as a function of context length and evidence position, from the length and position sweeps. This one has no runtime gauge. It is measured offline and tracked as an evaluation metric.

K2. Pinning means "this request is wrong without this item". If a pinned item fails permission, one of two things is true. Either the caller pinned data the user may not see, which is an upstream authorization bug, or the request cannot be answered correctly for this user. Dropping the item silently would hide the bug and send a prompt the caller considers incomplete. Raising makes the bug visible where it happened and fails the request before any data reaches the model. Non-pinned items are optional by definition, so dropping them for permission is correct behavior and is recorded in the manifest.

K3. The notice is part of the stable system prefix. If it appeared only when untrusted items were present, requests with and without evidence would have different prefixes. That splits the prefix cache in two and changes the hash the team monitors. A constant notice costs a few dozen tokens, which are themselves cached, and it keeps the prefix byte-identical for every request on a prompt version. It is also harmless when no untrusted block is present.

K4. Any three of the following. Identifiers such as ticket ids, asset tags, and account numbers live in structured facts set by code from tool results or systems of record. Monetary amounts and quantities also live in structured facts, with units and provenance (source_turn). Commitments made to the user ("we will call back by Friday") and decisions live in facts of category commitment or decision, or in the system of record they belong to, such as the ticket. Secrets and credentials do not belong in context at all, and they stay in a secret store. Code patches, configuration, and legal clauses stay as verbatim artifacts in storage, referenced by id and rehydrated when needed. In every case the append-only turn log remains the source of truth behind the structured copy.

K5. A cap limits how much a section can take. A floor guarantees how much a section keeps when another section's items have higher priority. Without a history floor, enough high-scoring evidence fills the budget before any turn is considered, because turns usually have lower priority than a top retrieval hit. The Northwind example: a user asks about laptop replacement, then sends "can I get it this week?". Retrieval returns twelve long chunks with scores above 0.9. Without a floor, the two previous turns are dropped, and "it" has no referent. With a floor of a few hundred tokens, the recent turns survive, and the lowest-ranked evidence is dropped with reason reserved_for_other_sections.

K6. Any two of the following. The provider has a minimum cacheable prefix length that the stable prefix does not reach. The provider requires explicit cache markers, and the request does not set them. The cache entry expires between requests because traffic per prompt version is low. Requests are spread across regions or replicas whose caches are separate. Content the builder does not see is placed before the system message and varies, such as tool definitions rendered by the gateway in a non-deterministic order, so the provider's token prefix differs even though the builder's hash does not. The model or adapter version changed between requests, for example through a fallback in the gateway.

K7. First marker after the system section, including tool definitions, schemas, and the constant untrusted-data notice. It is identical for every request on this prompt version, so every request reuses it. Second marker after the conversation state at the end of the system message. State changes only on compaction or a fact change, so consecutive turns of one session reuse the prefix through the state. Third marker after the last history turn. History is append-only between compactions, so the next turn of the same session reuses everything up to that point and pays full price only for the turns added since (the previous question and its answer), the tool results, the evidence, and the request. Nothing after the history is worth marking, because evidence and the request change on every request. After a compaction, the state and history markers miss once and the system marker still hits. If the system section is below the provider's minimum cacheable length, the first marker earns nothing on its own, and the second and third still can.

docs.title: Engineering questions
docs.text:
E1. Assumptions (illustrative): a 4,000-token base consisting of system prompt and tool specs, tool results averaging 2,000 tokens with a maximum of 4,000, 200 tokens of model output per step, and 30 steps.

Policy:

  • Facts, exact and pinned. Incident id, affected services and hosts, error signatures and codes, timestamps of the first and last error, the deploy or change ids found, and each hypothesis with its status (confirmed or ruled out), plus the evidence id for that status. These are set by code from parsed tool results where possible.
  • Step ledger, compact and verbatim. One line per completed step: tool, key arguments, outcome, and the reference to the stored full result. About 60 tokens per step.
  • Summary, narrative. How the investigation progressed and why the current hypothesis is preferred. Guarded as in the chapter.
  • Verbatim. The last two tool results in full, and any result whose step returned an error, until the error is resolved.
  • Trigger. Compact when verbatim tool output exceeds 10,000 tokens, and compact down to the last two results. Run compaction after a step completes, never in the middle of a step.

Without compaction, step k sends about 4,000 + 2,200k tokens, so 30 steps send about 30 × 4,000 + 2,200 × 465 ≈ 1.14 million input tokens. With the policy, the per-step input is bounded by roughly 4,000 + 500 facts + 800 summary + 8,000 verbatim worst case + 1,800 ledger at 30 steps ≈ 15,000 tokens, which is at most about 450,000 in total and usually far less. The per-step cost is roughly flat, not linear in k. Acceptance: a replay of recorded incident runs shows equal or better task success, and every identifier used in the final report appears in facts or in a rehydrated result.

E2. Both are volatile per request or per user. They go in the volatile tail: the final user message or a short "request context" block placed after the history, never in the system section. The system contract can say "the user's display name and today's date are provided with each request", which is constant text. Tests: lint_stable_items in CI over every prompt version's stable items, which flags dates and timestamps. A stability test builds two requests for different users on different dates and asserts identical prefix_hash values. The name needs its own check, because the lint has no pattern for names. Build with two different user names and assert that the stable prefix contains neither name.

E3. Places: the raw turn log, which is the source of truth; a fact, if the application stored it as one; the current summary, if the summarizer narrated it; earlier summaries, if summary versions are retained; trace spans that store prompt bodies; provider-side logs, under the provider's retention terms; any cross-session memory store (Chapter 21); and response caches keyed by prompts that contained it. Procedure: redact the turn in the log and keep a tombstone with the deletion request id. Call forget(key) on any fact holding it, and purge fact_history entries for that key. Rebuild the summary from the redacted log with rebuild_summary, because editing the summary text in place is unreliable, and run the literal guard so the number cannot reappear. Delete or redact stored prompt bodies in traces, keeping manifests, which hold no content. Invalidate response-cache entries for the session. Delete matching memory records. Confirm by running a retrieval and summary search for the number, which must return nothing. Prefix caches on the provider expire on their own and contain no state that later requests can retrieve, but document this in the deletion record.

E4. Raising the cap risks lost-in-the-middle failures and distraction, plus high cost and latency per question. It works only if the model's position curve is flat at that length. Retrieval over sections risks missing the clause that answers the question when the question's wording differs from the contract's, or when the answer needs two distant clauses, such as a definition and an obligation. Map-reduce summaries risk losing exactly the precise clauses that contract questions need, and they cost a full pass per document. Evaluation: a question set written by someone who knows the contract, covering single-clause lookups, multi-clause reasoning, and definition-dependent questions, with gold clause ids. Measure answer accuracy, citation correctness against the gold clauses, cost, and latency for each design. In practice, retrieval with section-aware chunking plus a definitions section pinned per document tends to win. Raising the cap can serve as a fallback for questions that fail retrieval, but only if the position sweep at that length supports it.

docs.title: Practical exercises
docs.text:
P1. Expected implementation: compact_tool_result(item: ContextItem, fields: list[str], store: dict[str, str]) -> ContextItem. It parses item.content as JSON, extracts the dotted paths ("ticket", "items.0.id"), stores the original in store under a key such as the item id, and returns a new item with the trimmed JSON, the same source_id with a #trimmed suffix, the same trust (untrusted), and metadata={"full_ref": key, **item.metadata}. Missing paths are recorded as null, not skipped, so the model can see that the field was absent. Acceptance criteria: required fields have equal values before and after; the trimmed item's token count is lower for a realistic result; store[item.metadata["full_ref"]] equals the original content; ACL metadata is preserved, so acl_filter behaves identically; non-JSON content raises a clear error instead of being truncated.

P2. Expected implementation: ContextBuilder(..., restate: str | None = None, restate_after_tokens: int = 4000). After allocation, if the estimated size exceeds the threshold, _render adds the restatement line inside the final user message, before Request:. It is not added to the system message. Its tokens must be reserved in allocation: count it as a fixed cost when the threshold could be crossed, or allocate twice. Acceptance criteria: the hash for a small build equals the hash for a large build with restate enabled; the line appears only above the threshold; the line sits immediately before the request; the budget test still holds with the line included; the manifest or span records context.restated = true.

P3. Expected implementation: a script under context/experiments/attribution.py. For each evaluation case (question, candidate items, expected answer), it builds the full prompt and records the answer from a FakeLLM handler. The handler answers only if a specific source id is present in the prompt, for example by mapping source ids to facts and composing an answer from the facts present. Then, for each included evidence item, it rebuilds without that item and records whether the answer changed. Output: per item, the number of cases where it was included and where its removal changed the answer. Items with zero changes across all inclusions are flagged. Acceptance criteria: on a synthetic set where one item is decisive and two are distractors, the decisive item is reported as influential and the distractors as never influential; the script uses ContextBuilder for every build, never manual string assembly; it runs offline.

P4.
